member.name: M:NAudio.Dsp.BiQuadFilter.Transform(System.ReadOnlySpan{System.Single},System.Span{System.Single})
member.summary: Passes a block of samples through the filter. Equivalent to — and produces byte-identical output to — calling on each element of in order, but keeps the coefficients and state variables in locals so the JIT can hold them in registers across the loop.
member.param: Output samples. May be the same span as (in-place filtering) or a separate buffer at least as long as .
member.remarks: A biquad has a forward-only dependency (the next output depends on previous inputs AND outputs), so the inner loop can't be vectorised; the speedup over the single-sample form comes entirely from not having to reload field values each iteration.

member.name: M:NAudio.Dsp.BiQuadFilter.ResetState
member.summary: Clears the filter's sample history (the x/y delay elements) without changing its coefficients, so the next input is filtered as if from silence. Use when reusing a filter on a new, unrelated signal (e.g. an effect's Reset()).

member.name: M:NAudio.Dsp.BiQuadFilter.SetLowPassFilter(System.Single,System.Single,System.Single)
member.summary: Set this up as a low pass filter
member.param: Q (quality factor). Use 1/sqrt(2) ≈ 0.707 for a Butterworth response (maximally flat passband, no peaking) — the recommended default for a clean low-pass. Larger values produce a resonant peak at the cutoff; smaller values give a more gradual roll-off into the cutoff. The slope above the cutoff is ~12 dB/octave regardless of Q — cascade biquads in series for a steeper roll-off.

member.name: M:NAudio.Dsp.BiQuadFilter.UpdateLowPassFilter(System.Single,System.Single,System.Single)
member.summary: Retunes this filter to a new low-pass cutoff and Q without clearing its sample history, so a running filter can be modulated every sample/block (e.g. a synth filter envelope or LFO, an auto-wah) without the click that causes by resetting state. Use only on an already-running, non-divergent filter; for a fresh filter or after a seek use (or ) so latched NaN/Infinity can't survive.

member.name: T:NAudio.Dsp.DahdsrEnvelope
member.summary:
Six-stage DAHDSR (Delay, Attack, Hold, Decay, Sustain, Release) envelope generator. This generalises the four-stage with the extra Delay and Hold stages that SoundFont and SFZ instruments require, and a seconds-based API (stage durations are set in seconds rather than raw rates). The output is a linear amplitude/modulation multiplier in the range [0, 1].
The attack is convex (an exponential approach toward an over-shoot target), matching the SoundFont volume-envelope attack shape. Decay and release are constant-rate ramps following the SoundFont "time for a 100% change" semantic (SF2.04 §8.1.2): the stage time sets the ramp's rate, and the level the ramp runs to (the sustain level for decay, silence for release) truncates it, so a smaller change completes proportionally sooner. The ramp shape is selectable via : exponential in amplitude (a constant fall in dB — the volume-envelope shape, gens 36/38) or linear in value (the modulation-envelope shape, gens 28/30). Designed for allocation-free real-time use.

member.summary: Decay time in seconds. Per the SoundFont semantic (SF2.04 §8.1.2 gens 36/28) this is the time for a 100% change — full scale down to -100 dB (exponential shape) or to zero (linear shape) — and sets the ramp's rate; the sustain level truncates the ramp, so a high sustain is reached proportionally sooner (e.g. a 2 s decay to a -1 dB sustain completes in 2 s x 1/100 = 20 ms).

member.summary: Release time in seconds. Like the decay this is the time for a 100% change (SF2.04 §8.1.2 gens 38/30), so it sets the ramp's rate and releasing from below full scale completes proportionally sooner — e.g. releasing from a -20 dB sustain takes (80/100) x ReleaseSeconds with the exponential shape.

member.name: M:NAudio.Dsp.DahdsrEnvelope.Advance(System.Int32)
member.summary: Advances the envelope by samples in one call and returns the new output value, leaving , and bit-identical to calling that many times. The delay and hold counters are consumed in O(1); the attack/decay/release ramps are stepped per sample within the active stage with the state hoisted to locals — a closed-form Math.Pow skip would drift from the repeated per-sample float multiplies by more than 1 ulp, so exact per-stage stepping is used instead, which still removes the per-sample call and field-traffic overhead. Intended for control-rate consumers that read the envelope once per block.
member.param: Number of samples to advance by. Must not be negative.

member.name: T:NAudio.Dsp.FftProcessor
member.summary:
A reusable FFT processor specialised for fixed-size real-input audio work. Compared to calling directly, this class:
Uses an N/2-point complex FFT plus an unpack pass to compute an N-point real FFT, returning an N/2 + 1-bin half-spectrum. Roughly half the work of the full complex FFT for the same N.
Precomputes the window coefficients (if configured) so the time-domain window is applied with one multiply per sample instead of a fresh cos evaluation.
Exposes APIs so callers can pass stack-allocated or pooled buffers.
member.remarks: Scaling matches : applies a 1/N scale (so a DC signal of magnitude 1 yields spectrum[0].Real = 1). is un-scaled, so RealInverse(RealForward(x)) recovers x.

member.name: T:NAudio.Dsp.InterpolatingSampleReader
member.summary: Reads a at an arbitrary, per-sample-varying playback rate with interpolation, honouring the source's loop mode. This is the core pitch-shifting primitive of the sampler/synth: each voice owns one reader and supplies a playback increment (in source samples per output sample) that may change every sample under vibrato, pitch-bend or a pitch envelope. Unlike (a fixed-ratio block resampler), the increment is free to move continuously. Allocation-free in steady state.

member.name: P:NAudio.Dsp.Lfo.StartPhase
member.summary: The phase, as a fraction of a cycle in [0, 1), that the oscillator starts from. Setting it moves the current phase there immediately (like , which also re-applies it); values outside [0, 1) wrap. The default of 0 keeps the historical behaviour (triangle and square start at +1, sine and sawtooth rising through their zero / minimum). Because the phase does not advance during , the first sample after the delay expires is taken at this phase — a SoundFont LFO (SF2.04 §8.1.2 gens 21/23) "begins its upward ramp from zero" when its delay elapses, which for the triangle waveform is a start phase of 0.75.

member.name: P:NAudio.Dsp.Lfo.DelaySeconds
member.summary: An optional delay in seconds before the LFO starts oscillating. During the delay outputs 0 (the bipolar neutral value), matching the SoundFont/SFZ LFO delay behaviour. The delay is re-armed by .

member.name: M:NAudio.Dsp.Lfo.Advance(System.Int32)
member.summary: Advances the oscillator by samples in one call, returning the value the last of that many calls would have returned (0 while the delay is still running; for = 0 the state is untouched and the value the next call will return is reported). The resulting state is bit-identical to repeated calls: the delay countdown is consumed in O(1), and the phase accumulator is stepped with the same per-sample additions Process performs (a closed-form phase + n x increment would round differently), but the waveform — the dominant per-sample cost — is evaluated only once. Intended for control-rate consumers that read the LFO once per block.
member.param: Number of samples to advance by. Must not be negative.

member.name: T:NAudio.Dsp.LinkwitzRileyCrossover
member.summary: Linkwitz–Riley 4th-order (24 dB/oct) crossover that splits a single channel into N contiguous bands at N-1 ascending crossover frequencies. Each split is two cascaded Butterworth biquads (LR4); a two-band split sums back to a magnitude-flat (all-pass) response. For more than two bands the split is serial, which carries a small recombination ripple — fine for band-wise dynamics, which is its purpose. A reusable building block for multiband compression and the de-esser.

member.name: M:NAudio.Dsp.SynthMath.ResonanceCentibelsToQ(System.Double)
member.summary: Converts a SoundFont filter resonance (initialFilterQ) in centibels to a linear biquad Q value. The input is clamped to the spec range of 0..960 cB (SF2.04 §8.1.2 gen 8) so malformed values cannot reach float infinity. 0 cB means a flat, non-resonant response, so the mapping subtracts 3.01 dB before converting — Q = 10^((cB/10 - 3.01)/20) — giving the Butterworth Q of ~0.707 at 0 cB (the convention FluidSynth also documents for this generator).

member.name: T:NAudio.Dsp.VoiceActivityDetector
member.summary: Energy-based voice activity detector with an adaptive noise floor and hangover. Operates on a mono sample stream in fixed analysis frames: a frame counts as speech when its level rises a configurable margin above the tracked noise floor, and the decision is held for a short hangover so word-final sounds are not clipped. Used to gate noise-estimate updates (noise suppression), freeze AGC during silence, or drive a transmit gate.

member.name: T:NAudio.Effects.AudioEffect

member.name: T:NAudio.Effects.EffectChain
member.summary: An ordered chain of s exposed as a single . Effects are applied in the order they were added.
member.remarks: The chain may be edited (, , , ) from one thread while another thread calls : each edit publishes a new immutable array with a single atomic write, so a concurrent always sees either the pre- or post-edit chain, never a partial state, and never takes a lock. Edits are serialized against each other by an internal lock, so multiple editor threads are also safe. New effects are configured for the source format on the editing thread before they are published, so configuration never lands on the audio thread.

member.name: T:NAudio.Effects.LimiterEffect
member.summary: Brick-wall peak limiter with look-ahead and optional true-peak (inter-sample) detection. The signal is delayed by the look-ahead time while a channel-linked peak detector sees the audio early, so gain is already reduced by the time a transient reaches the output — no overshoot, no audible pumping from a hard catch. With enabled the detector measures the oversampled signal, so reconstruction (inter-sample) peaks are caught too. Gain recovers with a smooth release. Reports its look-ahead as for delay compensation.

member.name: T:NAudio.Effects.ParameterDispatchQueue
member.summary: Lock-free single-producer/single-consumer queue that carries parameter writes from a control thread (UI, automation, presets) to the audio thread. The producer calls — invoked for you by once the parameter has been ed — and the audio thread calls once at the top of each processing block. Every pending write is then applied on the audio thread, so coefficient recomputation, delay-buffer resizes and filter swaps happen where there is no concurrent reader.
member.remarks: Both and are allocation-free and wait-free. The queue is intended for exactly one producer thread and one consumer thread, which matches the realtime harness (a single UI dispatcher and one audio callback). It is bounded: when full, drops the write — the next edit of the same parameter supersedes it anyway, and at audio-block rate the queue never approaches full under human-rate edits.

member.name: T:NAudio.Effects.SendBus
member.summary:
An auxiliary effect send/return bus: a shared interleaved buffer that sources mix a portion of their signal into, run through one (typically a reverb or chorus), with the wet result returned (added) into a destination mix.
This is the generic plumbing a mixer or sampler uses to share one reverb or chorus instance across many voices, rather than instantiating the effect per voice. The effect runs every block so its tail keeps sounding after the sends stop. Not thread-safe; drive it from the audio thread.

member.name: P:NAudio.Effects.SendBus.IdleTimeoutFrames
member.summary: How long (in frames) the effect keeps running after the last block of written input, i.e. a conservative upper bound on its audible tail. While input keeps arriving the effect always runs; once input has been silent for this long, skips the effect entirely until input is written again. 0 (the default) disables idle skipping — the effect runs every block.

member.name: P:NAudio.Effects.SendBus.IsIdle
member.summary: Whether the bus is currently idle: idle skipping is enabled and the tail window since the last written input has fully elapsed (a fresh bus starts idle — it has no tail to flush).

member.summary: Runs the effect over the accumulated send signal and adds the wet result into (the dry mix). Call once per block after sources have written their sends via . This overload assumes input may have been written, so the effect always runs (and any idle countdown re-arms).

member.name: T:NAudio.Wave.SampleProviders.AdsrSampleProvider
member.summary: Applies an ADSR (attack / decay / sustain / release) amplitude envelope to a source sample provider. Wraps , exposing its stage times in seconds and its sustain level, and multiplies the source by the envelope each sample.
member.remarks: The envelope holds at once the attack and decay have completed, until is called to enter the release phase. Once the release finishes the envelope is idle, returns 0 (so the provider self-evicts from a ), and is raised.

member.name: M:NAudio.Wave.SampleProviders.AdsrSampleProvider.#ctor(NAudio.Wave.ISampleProvider,System.Boolean)
member.summary: Creates a new AdsrSampleProvider with default values (fast attack, no decay, full sustain, 0.3s release).
member.param: The source to apply the envelope to. Any channel count is supported.

When true (the default) the envelope's gate opens immediately, so the note begins its attack as soon as playback starts — matching the previous behaviour of this class. Set to false to arm the provider without starting it and trigger the note later with ; note that while idle returns 0, so do not initialise a player directly on an un-started provider and treat that as end-of-stream.

member.summary: Defines common channel mixing matrices for use with .
member.remarks: Each matrix has one row per input channel and one column per output channel. The values returned are fresh copies, so callers may mutate them without affecting other callers.

member.name: P:NAudio.Wave.SampleProviders.ChannelMixMatrix.MonoToStereo
member.summary: Converts a mono source to a 2-channel source by copying the input to both outputs.

member.summary: Converts a 2-channel source to a mono source by mixing the channels together using equal weight.

member.name: P:NAudio.Wave.SampleProviders.ChannelMixMatrix.StereoLeft
member.summary: Modifies a 2-channel stream by selecting only the first channel. The output is 2-channel.

member.name: P:NAudio.Wave.SampleProviders.ChannelMixMatrix.StereoRight
member.summary: Modifies a 2-channel stream by selecting only the second channel. The output is 2-channel.

member.name: P:NAudio.Wave.SampleProviders.ChannelMixMatrix.StereoTo5_1
member.summary: Converts a 2-channel source to a canonical 5.1 output. The output has 6 channels: FrontLeft, FrontRight, Center, Sub, RearLeft, RearRight, in that order.
member.remarks:
The matrix is designed so that the aggregate output volume from the 6-channel output is the same output volume that would've occurred if the original input was applied to two channels; if the original audio would've produced 200W of output spread across 2 speakers, the transformed output would also produce 200W of output, instead spread across 6 speakers.
This can be noted by the fact that no column in the matrix sums to 1.0. The loudest channel is the center channel, receiving a sum of 0.444 of its inputs (0.222 from left, 0.222 from right).
If you would like a matrix that maximizes output volume, scale the matrix by a factor of 2.25. One might do this to preserve entropy during processing, with a final gain reduction step at the output to maintain intended power output.

member.summary:
Author: Freefall Date: 05.08.16 Based on: the port of Stephan M. Bernsee´s pitch shifting class Port site: https://sites.google.com/site/mikescoderama/pitch-shifting Test application and github site: https://github.com/Freefall63/NAudio-Pitchshifter
NOTE: I strongly advice to add a Limiter for post-processing. For my needs the FastAttackCompressor1175 provides acceptable results: https://github.com/Jiyuu/SkypeFX/blob/master/JSNet/FastAttackCompressor1175.cs

member.name: P:NAudio.Wave.SampleProviders.SmbPitchShiftingSampleProvider.LatencySamplesPerChannel
member.summary: The latency (group delay) introduced by the underlying STFT phase vocoder, expressed as a number of samples per channel. The shifted output is delayed by this many samples relative to the input, and the equivalent number of samples is lost from the tail when the source ends. The value is fftSize - fftSize / osamp and depends only on the FFT size and oversampling factor passed to the constructor (not on the pitch factor).
member.remarks: Use this to time-align pitch-shifted material with unshifted material, e.g. by skipping this many samples per channel from the start of the shifted output (see for the interleaved count to pass to an ).

member.name: P:NAudio.Wave.SampleProviders.SmbPitchShiftingSampleProvider.LatencySamples
member.summary: The latency (group delay) introduced by the underlying STFT phase vocoder, expressed as an interleaved sample count (latency per channel multiplied by the channel count). This is the value to use for when realigning pitch-shifted audio with unshifted audio.

member.summary: The latency (group delay) introduced by the underlying STFT phase vocoder, expressed as a .

member.name: T:NAudio.Wave.WaveFormat
member.summary: Represents a Wave file format
member.remarks: Not an interop type. It once carried [StructLayout] and was marshalled directly as a WAVEFORMATEX, but a class hierarchy cannot be marshalled correctly under Native AOT — the inherited fields are dropped, so a subclass decodes from offset 0 with its base fields left at their defaults. Use , or to cross a native boundary. See https://github.com/naudio/NAudio/issues/1432.

member.summary: Creates a new WaveFormatExtensible with full control over the SubFormat, valid bits per sample and channel mask. Use this overload when the convenience PCM/IEEE constructor's assumptions don't fit — for example to create 32-bit integer PCM (rather than IEEE float), to carry a container size that differs from the valid bit depth (e.g. 24 valid bits in a 32-bit container), or to preserve an explicit channel layout.

Number of valid bits per sample (may be less than )
Channel mask describing the speaker layout, or 0 if unspecified

member.summary: Creates a new linear PCM or IEEE float WaveFormatExtensible, choosing the SubFormat from . Use this convenience overload when you don't need an arbitrary SubFormat GUID but still want control over valid bits and channel mask — in particular it can create 32-bit integer PCM ( false), which the bit-depth-based constructor cannot.
member.param: Container bits per sample (block alignment is derived from this)
True for IEEE float samples, false for integer PCM

Channel mask describing the speaker layout, or 0 if unspecified

member.summary: An audio source that provides 32-bit floating-point samples, whatever the format of the underlying audio.

remarks.para: supplies raw bytes in the source's own format (for example 8, 16, 24 or 32-bit PCM, or floating point), so code that processes samples must handle each format separately. always supplies interleaved 32-bit floating-point samples, nominally in the range -1.0 to 1.0, so effects, mixers and meters only need to be written once. member.name: T:NAudio.Wave.IWaveLatency
member.summary: Interface for audio players and captures that can report the latency between a sample entering the audio pipeline and emerging from (or being delivered by) the hardware. Implement alongside or to let downstream code synchronise visualisations, lighting, video, recording timecode, or any other time-aligned consumer with audible output or captured input.

remarks.para: Latency values are only meaningful during uninterrupted operation. When the device is stopped or paused, or when an underrun has occurred, implementations should return their best steady-state estimate rather than throw — consumers driving visualisations need a stable value to fall back on.

The two properties answer different questions. describes the pipeline (it changes only when buffer settings change), so it is the right value for scheduling. describes the live state of the pipeline at this instant and is the right value for drift detection or per-frame correction.

may be computed either as the forward queue depth (e.g. WASAPI GetCurrentPadding divided by sample rate — "if I queued a sample now, this is how long until I'd hear it") or as the wall-clock age of the sample currently at the play / capture head (timestamping each buffer fill). The two values converge in steady state and diverge only under irregular feed patterns; this interface deliberately permits either, so implementations can use whichever the underlying driver exposes most cheaply.

For drivers whose buffer scheduling is fully predictable (notably ASIO, which always swaps fixed-size buffers at regular intervals), may simply return . The approximation is exact to within half a buffer.

member.name: P:NAudio.Wave.IWaveLatency.AverageLatency
member.summary: The steady-state latency from a sample being queued for output to it being emitted by the audio hardware, assuming uninterrupted playback. This is a property of the buffer configuration and the driver, not of the current playback state.

member.name: P:NAudio.Wave.IWaveLatency.CurrentLatency
member.summary: The time that has elapsed since the sample currently emerging from the hardware was queued for output. In steady state this is approximately equal to ; it differs during start-up, after an underrun, or when the host is filling buffers irregularly. Implementations that cannot meaningfully distinguish from the average are permitted to return .

You called the method.

The provided instance has reached its end (no more samples to play).

member.name: T:NAudio.Wave.SampleProviderBase
member.summary: Base class for creating an by overriding a Read(float[], int, int) method instead of . Like it also implements , so a derived class can be passed straight to an .

remarks.para: This exists for callers that cannot express in a method signature. The most common case is VB.NET, whose compiler rejects any source that names a ref struct ("Types with embedded references are not supported in this version of your compiler"), making and impossible to implement directly. It is also a convenient landing point when porting NAudio 2 code, whose Read had this exact signature.
The bridge rents a buffer from and copies once per read, so C# code should prefer implementing or deriving from directly and avoid the extra copy.
remarks.example:
In VB.NET:
Public Class SineProvider Inherits SampleProviderBase
Public Sub New() MyBase.New(44100, 1) End Sub
Public Overrides Function Read(buffer() As Single, offset As Integer, count As Integer) As Integer For i = 0 To count - 1 buffer(offset + i) = 0.0F Next Return count End Function End Class

member.name: T:NAudio.Wave.WaveProviderBase
member.summary: Base class for creating an of any format by overriding a Read(byte[], int, int) method instead of .

remarks.para: This exists for callers that cannot express in a method signature. The most common case is VB.NET, whose compiler rejects any source that names a ref struct ("Types with embedded references are not supported in this version of your compiler"), making impossible to implement directly. It is also a convenient landing point when porting NAudio 2 code, whose Read had this exact signature.

If your provider produces 32 bit float samples, prefer , which also implements so it can be used in a sample pipeline. If you need seeking and a length, derive from instead — its inherited overload is likewise overridable without naming a span.
The bridge rents a buffer from and copies once per read, so C# code should prefer implementing directly and avoid the extra copy.

member.summary: Returns true if reflects the exact frame-summed sample count, false if it is an estimate from the first frame's bitrate. False is only possible for headerless VBR files; CBR files and VBR files with a Xing/Info header report true immediately after the constructor returns.

member.name: M:NAudio.Wave.Mp3FileReaderBase.EnsureExactLengthAsync(System.Threading.CancellationToken)
member.summary: Forces a full scan of the MP3 frame index so reports the exact frame-summed sample count and returns true. No-op (returns a completed task) if Length is already exact — which it is from the constructor for CBR files and for VBR files carrying a Xing/Info header. Safe to call concurrently with Read and changes; scan is serialised against playback by the same internal lock. Restores the current playback position when complete.
member.remarks: This is about only — it is not a prerequisite for seeking. extends the frame index on demand whatever this reports.

member.name: T:NAudio.Wave.WaveStream
member.summary:
The base class for seekable (repositionable) audio sources.
Derives from , and implements so that it can be directly consumed by the entire NAudio audio processing pipeline.
Typically, this is used by file format readers, such as the .

para.b: Building a new audio capable class: or — what is more suitable to use and when?

remarks.para:
The class is suitable to be used as a base class when you are providing a new source into the NAudio audio pipeline that has immutable audio - that is, audio whose samples are not changed and their exact count is known once the object is initialized. File format readers is a primary example.
By contrast, suits a component that wraps another and manipulates the audio samples in some way.
Using is also suitable when building any signal generator.

para.b: Implementing a WaveStream — which Read method should I override?

remarks.para: is abstract on and must be overridden. is virtual — its default implementation rents a buffer from , calls the byte[] overload, and copies into the span. This is functionally correct but incurs one pool rent and one extra copy per read.

member.name: P:NAudio.Wave.WaveStream.WaveFormat
member.summary: Retrieves the for this wave stream.
member.remarks:
The audio format describes the wave data that are provided by successive calls.
Without this, it is not possible to know how the audio samples are laid out.
For most NAudio implementations, this typically returns a PCM or an IEEE floating-point format.

member.name: T:NAudio.Sfz.SfzMappedRegion
member.summary:
An SFZ region with its Tier-1 and Tier-2 opcodes interpreted into typed, engine-ready synthesis parameters: absolute key/velocity ranges (note names resolved, offsets applied), tuning in cents, volume in dB, pan normalised to ±1, the amplitude envelope in seconds, the filter, loop behaviour, sample offsets, group/trigger routing, note-on selection (keyswitches, round-robin, random and CC windows), crossfades, the per-region LFOs/EGs and EQ bands, effect sends and release decay.
This is the SFZ semantic layer, the counterpart to the SoundFont generator model. It does not load samples or touch the voice engine — projecting both formats onto one neutral model the engine plays is the next step.

member.name: M:NAudio.Sfz.SfzMappedRegion.Map(NAudio.Sfz.SfzRegion,System.Int32,System.Int32)
member.summary: Interprets a parsed 's opcodes. The and (from the instrument's <control> section) transpose incoming MIDI notes; here that is realised by shifting the explicitly specified key-valued opcodes the opposite way.
member.remarks: key versus explicit lokey/hikey/pitch_keycenter: strict SFZ semantics apply opcodes in document order (the later one wins), but the merged opcode set this maps from no longer carries that order. This mapping deliberately deviates with a pragmatic rule: key supplies defaults for whichever of the three are not explicitly present, and an explicit opcode always wins regardless of where it was written — so <group> key=36 <region> lokey=35 hikey=37 keeps the region's range, with the keycenter defaulting from key.

member.name: M:NAudio.Sfz.SfzMappedRegion.BuildVelocityCurve
member.summary: Resolves into a full 128-entry curve indexed by MIDI velocity: defined points give their level, undefined velocities are linearly interpolated between the nearest defined neighbours — from (0, 0) below the lowest defined point and to (127, 1) above the highest, unless velocity 127 is itself defined. Returns null when the region defines no points; the resolved curve replaces the default velocity-squared term inside the amp_veltrack law.

member.name: T:NAudio.Sfz.SfzParser
member.summary:
Parses SFZ instrument files into an : handles comments, the #define/$variable preprocessor, #include, the section headers and the opcode=value grammar (including sample paths that contain spaces), then flattens the global/master/group/region hierarchy into playable regions.
A < always starts a header, even without surrounding whitespace (<group><region>, <region>sample=a.wav), matching real players' behaviour; consequently a sample path may contain spaces but never <.
This is the text/structure layer only — opcode semantics (key ranges, tuning, envelopes…) and external sample loading are applied by later layers on top of the parsed model.

member.name: P:NAudio.Sfz.SfzParser.DefineRegex
member.remarks:
Pattern:
^\\s*#define\\s+(\\$[A-Za-z0-9_]+)\\s+(.+?)\\s*$
Explanation:
○ Match if at the beginning of the string.
○ Match a whitespace character atomically any number of times.
○ Match the string "#define".
○ Match a whitespace character atomically at least once.
○ 1st capture group.
○ Match '$'.
○ Match a character in the set [0-9A-Z_a-z] atomically at least once.
○ Match a whitespace character greedily at least once.
○ 2nd capture group.
○ Match a character other than '\n' lazily at least once.
○ Match a whitespace character greedily any number of times.
○ Match if at the end of the string or if before an ending newline.

member.name: P:NAudio.Sfz.SfzParser.IncludeRegex
member.remarks:
Pattern:
^\\s*#include\\s+"([^"]+)"\\s*$
Explanation:
○ Match if at the beginning of the string.
○ Match a whitespace character atomically any number of times.
○ Match the string "#include".
○ Match a whitespace character atomically at least once.
○ Match '"'.
○ 1st capture group.
○ Match a character other than '"' atomically at least once.
○ Match '"'.
○ Match a whitespace character greedily any number of times.
○ Match if at the end of the string or if before an ending newline.

member.name: P:NAudio.Sfz.SfzParser.VariableRegex
member.remarks:
Pattern:
\\$[A-Za-z0-9_]+
Explanation:
○ Match '$'.
○ Match a character in the set [0-9A-Z_a-z] atomically at least once.

member.name: P:NAudio.Sfz.SfzParser.BlockCommentRegex
member.remarks:
Pattern:
/\\*.*?\\*/
Options:
RegexOptions.Singleline
Explanation:
○ Match the string "/*".
○ Match any character lazily any number of times.
○ Match the string "*/".

member.name: P:NAudio.SoundFont.SoundFont.SampleData
member.summary: The raw Sample Data exactly as stored in the file's smpl chunk: the high 16 bits of each sample, little-endian. For 24-bit SoundFonts the least-significant 8 bits are stored separately in (the file keeps them in a parallel sm24 chunk so 16-bit players can ignore them). To get decoded samples at the font's full precision use .

member.name: P:NAudio.SoundFont.SoundFont.SampleData24
member.summary: The raw optional 24-bit extension data (the file's sm24 chunk: one byte per sample, the low 8 bits of each sample), or null if the SoundFont contains only 16-bit samples. Pairs one byte with each 16-bit sample in ; combine as (smpl16 << 8) | sm24, or use .

member.name: P:NAudio.SoundFont.SoundFont.Has24BitSamples
member.summary: Whether this SoundFont carries 24-bit sample data (an sm24 sub-chunk).

member.name: M:NAudio.SoundFont.SoundFont.ReadSampleDataFloat
member.summary: Decodes the sample pool to normalised 32-bit float at the font's full available precision: 16-bit samples from , extended with the low bytes from when the font is 24-bit (each sample is (smpl16 << 8) | sm24, scaled by 2^23). start/end/loop addresses index the result directly (one float per sample point). Allocates a new array on every call.

member.name: T:NAudio.SoundFont.SoundFontGenerators
member.summary:
A resolved set of SoundFont generator values, indexed by . Instances start from the SoundFont 2.04 default values (§8.1.3) and are then modified by zone generators during instrument resolution (see ).
Values are the raw signed generator amounts from the file; the units (cents, timecents, centibels, etc.) are interpreted by the synthesiser (see NAudio.Dsp.SynthMath). Range and index generators (KeyRange, VelocityRange, Instrument, SampleID) are not stored here — they drive zone selection and are surfaced on instead.

member.name: M:NAudio.SoundFont.SoundFontGenerators.CreateWithDefaults
member.summary: Creates a generator set initialised to the SoundFont 2.04 default values — the correct starting point for instrument-level resolution.

member.name: M:NAudio.SoundFont.SoundFontGenerators.CreateZeroed
member.summary: Creates a generator set with every value zero — the correct starting point for accumulating preset-level offsets, which are added to the instrument-level values.

member.name: P:NAudio.SoundFont.SoundFontGenerators.Item(NAudio.SoundFont.GeneratorEnum)
member.summary: Gets or sets the raw value of a generator. Out-of-range generator enumerators read as 0 and ignore writes.

member.name: P:NAudio.SoundFont.SoundFontGenerators.OverridingRootKey
member.summary: The MIDI key that plays the sample at its recorded pitch (overridingRootKey), or -1 to use the sample header's original pitch.

member.name: P:NAudio.SoundFont.SoundFontGenerators.KeyNumberOverride
member.summary: A fixed key to use for this region regardless of the played note, or -1 (the default) to use the played note.

member.name: P:NAudio.SoundFont.SoundFontGenerators.VelocityOverride
member.summary: A fixed velocity to use for this region regardless of the played velocity, or -1 (the default) to use the played velocity.

member.name: P:NAudio.SoundFont.SoundFontGenerators.ExclusiveClass
member.summary: The exclusive (choke) class — notes sharing a non-zero exclusive class within a preset cut each other off (e.g. hi-hat open/closed). 0 = none.

member.name: T:NAudio.Sequencing.EventBufferQuery
member.summary: Stateless per-buffer event query — the dispatch math used by , exposed as a standalone API for consumers that don't want to route events through a (e.g. a VST3 instrument provider feeding events into a plugin's process() event input).
member.remarks: Stateless by design: the caller supplies an arbitrary [startFrame, endFrameExclusive) range, so a host that pulls e.g. 4096 frames from WASAPI can split the work across multiple downstream process() calls if the plugin's max block size is smaller. The dispatcher receives each event with its effective absolute tick (after the position transform and, in a loop, after iteration translation) and a sample-accurate frame offset relative to startFrame. Queries are audio-thread friendly: they run over the timeline's lock-free immutable snapshot (see ) and perform no heap allocations.

member.name: T:NAudio.Sequencing.EventTimeline`1
member.summary: An ordered set of timed events with a consumer-defined payload. Events are sorted by tick; events with the same tick preserve insertion order. Internally the timeline is an immutable snapshot array published copy-on-write: mutators (, ) serialise on an internal lock and atomically publish a new array, while queries read the current snapshot lock-free and (via ) allocation-free. This trade-off favours the audio thread — timelines are queried every buffer but mutated rarely (user edits) — at the cost of an O(n) copy per mutation, and it means a UI-thread edit can never block or priority-invert the audio thread's per-buffer query.

member.name: M:NAudio.Sequencing.EventTimeline`1.EventsInRangeSpan(System.Int64,System.Int64)
member.summary: The allocation-free, lock-free variant of : returns a span over the timeline's current immutable snapshot covering the half-open tick range [, ).
member.remarks: Safe to call from the audio thread while another thread mutates the timeline: a mutation publishes a new snapshot array, so the returned span stays valid and internally consistent (it keeps the snapshot it was created from) but does not observe later edits. Take a fresh span per buffer to pick up edits.
